analysis.one_liner: Bans state 'right-to-work' laws so unions can require dues as a job condition.
analysis.headline: The bill has not moved since it was introduced: it was referred to the Senate labor committee on September 4, 2025, and no hearing, vote, or further action has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently lets states pass 'right-to-work' laws, which ban union contracts that require workers to join or pay fees to a union as a condition of employment. 27 states have such laws. This bill repeals that authority, meaning unions would again be able to negotiate contracts requiring all covered workers to pay for union representation. It has been referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law and has not advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Union members and non-union workers in the 27 states with right-to-work laws. Unions would gain members and dues revenue, which they say funds stronger bargaining and enforcement; workers in covered workplaces could no longer opt out of paying for representation while still receiving union-negotiated wages and contract terms.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act, the provision that allows states to ban agreements requiring union membership or payment of union fees as a condition of employment [S2].

After repeal, unions in states that currently have right-to-work laws could negotiate union security agreements covering all workers in a bargaining unit, ending the situation where non-payers receive the same negotiated benefits as dues-payers [S2].

Supporters of union security argue it prevents 'free riding' and gives unions the resources to organize and enforce contracts; roughly half of US states currently have right-to-work statutes that this bill would preempt [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Unions' opponents and some individual workers bear the cost. Employers would face stronger, better-funded unions with more bargaining power. Workers who prefer not to join or pay a union could be required to do so to keep a job at a unionized workplace. Industries in states with lower union wage premiums could see labor costs rise.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and workers who don't want unions

drawbacks.text: Workers who decline union membership for personal, political, or financial reasons could be required to pay union fees as a condition of employment — the very requirement right-to-work laws prohibit [S2].
Employers, particularly in lower-wage right-to-work states, would face higher and more rigid labor costs as unions gain mandatory dues revenue and bargaining leverage [S1].

The bill overrides the policy choices of the 27 states that have enacted right-to-work laws, a central objection those states' elected officials have raised to federal preemption of labor policy [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades worker choice for union strength. Workers who value unions gain a dues-paying membership base that can bargain harder; workers who don't want to pay lose the option to opt out. The economic effect on wages and employment in right-to-work states is genuinely disputed, and the bill's main political obstacle is that its policy is directly opposite to the standing law of more than half the states.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat with no hearing or vote since September 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Nationwide Right To Unionize Act in the Senate on September 4, 2025 [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where it has remained with no further action [S4].
Fifteen senators, all Democrats or allied independents, cosponsored the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and union opponents in right-to-work states are better off, since the current law remains in place and nothing has changed. Union supporters are no worse off than before introduction.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 14 cosponsors.

against.name: Bill Cassidy
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee has taken no action on the bill since referral; no hearing or markup has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors are Democrats or allied independents; no Senate Republican has signed on, and Republicans hold a 55-47 majority in the Senate.

industries.note: Unions would gain the right to require dues from all covered workers in right-to-work states, increasing their revenue and membership. Union-backed advocacy argues this strengthens bargaining power and enforcement for the same workers who currently benefit without paying.

Employers would face union contracts that can require dues as a job condition, raising labor costs and narrowing management discretion. Some employers benefit from lower labor costs in right-to-work states, but a stronger union base can also raise wages for workers. This is the industry most directly targeted by the bill.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding a 55-47 Senate majority and the bill referred to a committee chaired by a Republican, it is highly unlikely to receive a hearing, markup, or floor vote this Congress. Comparable repeal efforts have stalled at the same stage in prior Congresses.
